title: Page blocks
description: New blocks for case studies and write-ups.

paragraphs:
Page blocks
11 November 2026

The modern schema has twenty block types, and text, titles and images account for about two thirds of what is actually on the pages. The blocks below are aimed at what the case studies and write-ups keep needing to say and currently say with a plain image and a paragraph.
Each would be a content-backed block: a schema entry, a renderer, and in-page editing. The prototypes show the reader’s side.
Design work is often a comparison: the old site and the new one, a render and the shipped product, light and dark. Two images side by side make the reader do the registration themselves.

One frame, two images, a divider you drag. The whole frame is the drag target and the control underneath is a native range input, so arrow keys, touch and screen readers work without extra code. The handle is the existing elevated surface, and the labels are the existing badge.
Drag anywhere on the image, or focus it and use the arrow keys.
The product case studies explain objects: which part does what, and why it is shaped that way. Today that is a photo followed by prose that says “the thumb slider” and trusts the reader to find it.

Numbered pins on the image, tied to a list beneath it. Pointing at either highlights both and quiets the rest. A click pins one. The list is ordinary page text, so it is readable with the image gone and it can be edited as text.
This is not the Draw layer. Draw is freehand commentary on top of any block; this is structured content that belongs to one image.
Hover a pin or a row. Click to keep one selected.

#88 asks for a case study to read in a few scrolls. Collapsing media into a carousel helps with images. It does nothing for the three paragraphs of research that half the readers want and half would skip.

A deep dive is a titled row that opens in place. Closed, it costs one line and says how much is inside. Open, its contents are ordinary blocks. It is a real disclosure button, the hidden content is inert until opened, and the height animates with grid rows, so nothing is measured in script.
Open either row.

Write-ups are a single 37.5em column, and on a desktop the space beside it is empty. The writing has asides in it: a caveat, a measurement’s conditions, a credit. In the column they interrupt; left out, they are lost.

A sidenote hangs in the margin, level with the sentence that cites it, in the optional-metadata ink. When the margin is not there, the same note opens in the flow under its paragraph when the reference is tapped. One block, two layouts, no footnote jump to the bottom of the page.
Hover a reference. Switch to Narrow and tap one.
#90 suggests images that look like they sit in familiar windows. Screenshots need it most: a bare screenshot has no edge against a white page and no sense of what it is a picture of.

I would make this a setting on the image block and not a new block: Frame, with None, Browser, App and Phone. The frames are drawn from tokens the system already has, including the traffic-light set from the panel header, so they stay quiet and they follow the theme.
Switch frames. Hover the window to wake the lights.
Figures row. Two to four numbers with a label each, in body type with tabular figures. For outcomes: units sold, milliseconds saved, awards. The bar chart demo already has the styling this needs.
Next project. #124 is about the project finale. The simplest good ending is the next project’s card at full column width.
Detached gallery card. #81 and #110 both want a card with no page behind it. That is a block on the listing page and not a project with a status of Image.

Sidenotes are the first block I would build for your own writing. Then the window frame, polished until its device and software chrome feels real. Deep dive, hotspots and before-and-after are parked until a project gives them a clear job.
